To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the ultrastructure of the gonadotrophic pituitary cells is not changed by antiandrogenic treatment, but that the number of cells and their secretory activity is increased.
cyproterone and aminoglutethimide cause an increase in the numbers of FSH- and ICSH-secreting gonadotroph cells and that these cells have the same structure as those of the castrated rat.

the gonadotropic cells in male rats after castration and after administration of cyproterone acetate and aminoglutethimide are enlarged, contain dilated rough endoplasmatic reticulum, enlarged Golgi complexes, decreased numbers of secretory granulae, and are more numerous in comparison with normal controls.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ultrastructural changes in the pituitary gonads after antiandrogen treatment and with the question whether the pituitary changes are similar to those found in castration.
a new aspect of the regulation of gonadotrophins.
the question of whether the pituitary gonadal axis is regulated by the hypothalamo-hypophyseal system alone or whether the pituitaries also play a role.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the antiandrogen treatment of the intact rat leads to a stimulation of the gonadotrophic function of the hypophysis, which is not due only to the hypothalamic release of gonadotrophine-releasing factors.
the ultrastructure of the pituitary gonado- trophs is influenced by androgen, and that this effect is mediated by the hypothalamo- hypophyseal system.
cyproterone acts on the pituitary gland in the same way as surgical castration and the administration of aminoglutethimide.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the gonadotropic cells of the rat adenohypohysis react to castration and to the administration of antiandrogens and of steroidogenesis inhibitors by a marked increase of their secretory activity.
cyproterone and aminoglutethimide are able to inhibit gonadotroph function, but not the structure and number of gonadotroph cells.
the gonadotropic cells of the rat hypophysis are stimulated by the gonadotropin-releasing factors and that this stimulation results in a hypertrophy of the gonadotrophic cell.
The main takeaway from our work is that
gonadotroph hyperplasia can be produced by chemical means, i. e., by antiandrogen treatment, without the intervention of the hypothalamus.
the gonadotropic cells are stimulated by the antiandrogens and the steroidogenesis inhibitors, but the stimulation is not as intense as in surgical castration.
the gonadotropic cells of the male pituitary gland can be differentiated from the gonadotropic cell types of the female pituitary gland by their ultrastructural characteristics.
